content.title: When Does The Pitt Season 2 Episode 13 Drop on HBO Max?
content.text: Andy Silva breaks down everything you need to know for the 13th episode of the second season of the critically acclaimed HBO Max show, starring Noah Wyle. The Pitt Season 2 Episode 13 premieres on Thursday, April 2, 2026, at 9 p.m. ET on HBO Max. Nearly everyone in the Pitt was pushed to the breaking point last week. Robby. Dana. Santos. Even Robby’s buddy Duke, who hit the nail on the head when he compared the PTMC ED to quicksand. Will any of our heroes be able to extract themselves from that quicksand before they snap? We’ll have to keep watching to find out, but I don’t know how much more rope any of them has after last week’s episode. The Pitt Season 2 Episode 13 Preview The end of the day is rapidly approaching and Robby says he just has a few more loose ends to tie up before heading out. But at the same time he still has so many things he needs to do, including worry about whether Dr. Al-Hashimi is fit to run the place and whether Langdon could relapse, especially as he is questioning whether he’s ready to be back in the ED. Not to mention have one last verbal sparring session with Dana. The open road may be calling — even if Robby’s lady friend Noelle won’t be joining him on his “vision quest” — but it looks like it’s going to have to wait just a little bit longer. The Pitt Season 2 Episode 12 Recap (Warning: Spoilers ahead.) Robby is at the end of his rope, and it’s evident throughout the episode. Whether it be how he responds to Dana after she defended Emma or his continued devil may care attitude about his upcoming increasingly ill-advised motorcycle journey or just watching him walk through the halls looking wrung out, Robby is not well. And everyone can see it. Dr. Al-Hashimi wants to recommend two attendings at all times because the ED is too much for just one person and McKay tries to pull from her own trauma overcoming addiction to warn Robby about getting too close to the edge. Duke recognizes that Robby feels like he needs to get out today because if he doesn’t, he may never get out. But it all finally comes to a head during his knock-down, drag-out fight with Dana where he says she hasn’t been right all day. She calls Robby on his BS, noting that he hasn’t been right all day either. She tells him what he needs to hear, not what he wants to hear, such as the fact he’s been ice cold to Langdon all day because he feels like Langdon let him down and because Langdon was his boy his failure is somehow a reflection on him. And she’s not here for Robby’s deflection about being worried the ED will fall apart without him, because the ED can and will survive without him, without Dana, without anyone. The ED doesn’t belong to him. More importantly, like McKay she accuses him of tempting death because he doesn’t care anymore. After all, elsewhere in this episode he spoke of Amor fati. We already saw at the end of last season that Robby was on the edge and had to be talked down. Unless something changes in the next couple of episodes, he may go over the edge. Of course, Dana isn’t in such good shape this week either. She bolts into action to defend Emma when the altered golf guy, Curtis, puts her in a headlock, perhaps roughing him up a bit along the way. Her own experience last season with Doug Driscoll is still weighing on her, as evidenced by the fact she happened to have some Versed in her pocket ready to go. She claims that’s not true, but Robby sees through it. He confronts Dana about it and she rails about the fact that if anyone else stops an assault like that they’re a hero but when a nurse does it they get punished. That being said, Dana goes into the bathroom and has a breakdown, so she knows she was playing with fire by going after the guy and is clearly still traumatized by her own assault last season. Robby is right that Dana is not herself, and certainly not the Dana of pre-Doug Driscoll, as evidenced by how she reacted when Emma was grabbed earlier this season. She and Robby fight multiple times in the episode, and it’s clear that all is not well between them heading into the final stretch of the season. Speaking of Curtis, his CT comes back clean. That’s the extent of his good news for him, however, as despite not realizing what he did he’s taking a ride downtown. Mixing beer and cocaine is no excuse for assaulting a medical worker, after all. But don’t feel too bad for Curtis — he’s no angel, even when sober. He loudly flips out at McKay, Dana and the entire Pitt once it becomes clear he’s going to face consequences. Even when McKay tries to help him, giving him some pamphlets about rehab, he reacts angrily. He’s just a jerk. Even when Robby is trying to be complimentary he’s off these days. He commends Mohan for how she handles her elderly couple, with one half played by Law & Order: SVU vet Dann Florek, and encourages her to go after an elective in geriatrics. But he ruins the moment by saying she has a predisposition for the pace, another slight aimed at her after her panic attack a few episodes back. Mohan continues to show a knack for actually listening to her patients, as she did last season with her sickle cell patient. Here, she finds a way to reasonably return the elderly couple to their home in a way that feels safe and could actually work, rather than just shuffling them off to assisted living (even if they may end up there anyways). Upon further reflection, I was a bit too hard on Santos last weekopens in a new tab. I especially felt that way after hearing her explain in a much better fashion why Langdon’s return has angered her so much. Last week she focused on the fact that he stole pills, which yes he did. But that’s a mistake he’s trying to make amends for. However, Santos has a point when she says she feels gaslit by the fact that everyone has welcomed Langdon back with open arms when even before she found out he stole pills he was a complete jerk to her on her first day as a doctor. It’s understandable why it would be hard to see everyone rally around someone who did treat you very badly, especially when you feel like for all the talk of the ED being family you’re getting thrown under the bus. I can understand why that would amplify her feelings of outrage that Langdon has simply walked back into the ED to a largely supportive welcome (well, except for Robby). It’s good see her be vulnerable with Whitaker and hopefully the fact that she clearly doesn’t want him to move out and actually likes living with him (even if she won’t come out and say it) will make him reconsider Robby’s offer to move into his place while he’s gone. And it looks like Santos may really need that, considering she subtly grabbed a scalpel, a sign that the pressure of the day may have her considering self-harm once again. Getting back to Langdon, it has perhaps been underplayed how big a deal it was for him to steal pills last season. Which is evident in how Dr. Al’s approach to Langdon changes when she finds out from Robby (accidentally, I think) that reason Langdon and Santos have beef is in part because she caught him stealing pills. Dr. Al is noticeably different toward Langdon through the rest of the episode, which does not go unnoticed. Langdon might have just lost his biggest champion at the moment. It also makes you wonder what happens if Santos gets her way and Langdon’s secret is revealed — how will the rest of the Pitt staff react? Langdon also has a moment with McKay, who despite trying to reach Robby has her own issues she’s dealing with. McKay is still processing the death of Roxie and how her two boys had to say goodbye to their mom, obviously leading McKay to think of her own son. She tells Langdon that she’s shut off her emotions for so long that she can’t remember the last time she cried and doesn’t even know if she’s capable of crying anymore. Of course, that doesn’t mean she wants a hug, Langdon. It puts into perspective something that Joy says to Langdon as she’s leaving for the day, even amid the ED’s chaos. She tells him that 62% of all ED docs report suffering from burnout. Joy thinks it means that all the “lunatics” in the Pitt need to learn how to set some boundaries, even if the nature of shows like The Pitt indicate that’s unlikely to happen anytime soon. Monica was needlessly nasty to Victoria in this episode, complaining about millennials and Gen Z and snowflakes and calling Victoria a “snowflake.” I think we all saw who the real “snowflake” was in that scenario. It’s a small moment, but kudos to Perlah for calming down the fireworks scalp lac guy’s brother so that he can get the help he needs. The Pitt has done a really nice job of showcasing the important work that both doctors and nurses do, with Perlah and Princess, in particular being standouts all season. The episode ends on a good news, bad news note. The good news —the cyber attacks seem to have been settled and the Pitt’s tech might be coming back online soon. Which mean, as Dr. Al puts it, that Robby is “cleared for take off.” But his friend Duke is still here, so it looks like he isn’t going to go rushing out the doors just yet. The bad news — Mohan’s diabetic patient from earlier in the day Orlando is back having fallen off a catwalk. Our docs just can’t catch a break. The Pitt FAQ What time do new episodes of The Pitt drop? New episodes of The Pitt drop on Thursdays at 9 p.m. ET. How can I watch new episodes of The Pitt ? The Pitt — including all of season 1 and season 2 to this point — is available to stream on HBO Max. Clips and behind-the-scenes featurettes are also uploaded to the HBO Max YouTube pageopens in a new tab. How many new episodes of The Pitt will drop in season 2? Season 2 of The Pitt is expected to include 15 episodes, with the season set to conclude on April 16, 2026.
